utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness Z: that is what you are going to be called throughout your testimony. Will you look at this piece of paper, which bears a name, and just say "yes" if the name is yours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may be satisfactory to deal with paragraph 1 in this way. Witness Z, have you summarised your career in the British army, or have you had summarised for you your career in the British army in the first three paragraphs of a summary served in this case, which I think you may have seen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In mid-December 1993, did you occupy a role in one of the ECMM teams, and again you have identified it in the summary. That team had areas of responsibility, including Travnik, Vitez and Busovaca and Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Head of the regional centre being Martin Garrod, and the head of the coordination centre being William Stutt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have been told which paragraphs I may and which paragraphs I may not lead on. And there follows a number of paragraphs where I may not lead. When you took up your position, Witness Z, were you introduced to the principal personalities in the Vitez pocket?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was, yes, during the week of handover between one monitor and myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I give some of the names, you can tell us what you understood them to be. Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. He was introduced as the HVO commanding officer for the Vitez pocket and for middle Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nikica Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nikica Petrovic was introduced to me on several occasions, but first introduced as the HVO liaison officer to Commander Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see you have a document before you. Are you looking from notes or are you looking at the summary that we have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am looking at the statement, the final summary that was prepared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Unless there is any objection to the witness having that. If there is, please let me know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: With respect to this witness, Your Honour, I do not believe that the witness, since she speaks and understands English extremely well, obviously, she doesn't need any kind of coaching material in front of you. So I would prefer that she did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think coaching material is exaggerating it. I can't really see any objection to a witness having a statement, when they are dealing with events which happened six or seven years ago. This is merely a summary of what she had. As far as possible, if, Witness Z, you can get on without it, do. But if you find that you can't remember, then that seems proper for you to refer to it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Darko Gelic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Darko Gelic was the liaison officer based in the Hotel Vitez, and he was working alongside Nikica Petrovic to Commander Blaskic in his absence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Santic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Santic was the mayor of Vitez, who I met once, twice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I turn to Dario Kordic, let's turn to the BiH Army side. Memhet Alagic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I met him on many occasions. He was the second in command, I believe, initially, which was called Corpus Brigada, which is 3rd Corps Brigade based in Zenica. And then he took over as the commander of 7th Brigade in Travnik in April of '94.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Enver Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the 2 IC of 3rd Brigade and took over as the leader eventually. I didn't meet him so many times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Samir Safic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Samir Safic was the exchange officer based in Travnik, responsible for live and dead body swaps on the Turbe-Travnik border and any negotiations with Nikica Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Beba Salko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Beba Salko was -- his role seems to change from day to day. Basically, he was in charge of removing Serbs from the Vitez pocket and also from Zenica, through the Vitez pocket, and was in close liaison with British battalions based in Vitez, again involved in the movement of live bodies as opposed to dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You will discover, Witness Z, that I leave a pause between questions and answers in order to make life possible and not difficult for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am going to deal with the first part of -- sorry, paragraph 6. I now turn to Dario Kordic. How was he introduced, and tell us a little bit about what you first learnt of him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I first met Dario Kordic in February, on the 16th of February, 1994. I was introduced to him through a series of events. I had been trying to facilitate the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. It's my mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you told he was? What title were you told was associated with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was told through various sources that Mr. Kordic was the head of the self-proclaimed party of Herceg-Bosna based in Mostar, but was actually running the Vitez pocket part of Herceg-Bosnia. I was told that he was a politician.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll come to your first meeting with him at the appropriate stage on a logical narrative. But you've given how he was described to you. Was he spoken of in similar terms or in different terms by the HVO liaison officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was never referred to as such, as a military commander, although it was mentioned from time to time that he had a position within the HVO. But, moreover, he was referred to as a political leader, especially one for the Vitez pocket. As a political leader.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please help us now with helicopter movements in general. We'll come to helicopter movements in particular cases later, but in general -- it's the first half of paragraph 7 and paragraph 8. Tell us about it, without referring to notes, if you can, because it will make your testimony much more vital.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In general, I was aware, as were many other airfield monitors, which of course I was one of to start with, that there was sufficient helicopter movement within the area of the Vitez pocket. There was absolutely no way that someone could move by road from Herceg-Bosnia area into Vitez. And the only guaranteed safe movement was by night, and was by helicopter movement. That was done by the HV and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When, so far as you were concerned, were these helicopter movements first taking place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was aware of them taking place on my arrival to the mission in August of 1993, but I didn't actually physically see any helicopter movements in the Vitez pocket until March of '94. But I was aware of them flying, because they were breaking the U.N. no-fly zone at the time, for which I was responsible for monitoring.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were your sources of information about helicopter movements, and when you've dealt with that, can you tell us what, if anything, you've discovered about the use of particular figures in the area of helicopters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was aware of helicopter movement because, prior to moving to Zenica, to middle Bosnia, I spent some time as an airfield monitor working with the U.N., a central nerve office, if you like, based in Zagreb. At that point they showed me how easy it was for the helicopters to move in and out of the base in Split, near Split, called basa Divulje, from a JNA barracks to middle Bosnia, because they are able to fly under their radar zone, therefore avoiding detection. Sorry, could you repeat the second part of the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your sources of intelligence or information about whether helicopters were being used, and by whom they were being used, and then tell us by whom they were being used.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vitez pocket is a very small area, and therefore those that were unable to move out of it had to do so by either road or by air. As the road was unaccessible -- only by the locals, rather. It was only accessible by ECMM and the U.N. and the military and a couple of non-government organisations. It was common knowledge -- and when I say "common knowledge," I base my sources on my interpreter, other interpreters that were working for ECMM, of which there are about 10 or 15, and I was basing my sources -- basing my information on sources that were working in the Hotel Vitez. And also I was being questioned constantly about helicopter movement by the army of BiH and General Alagic himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your common -- sorry. Wait for the interpreter. And your common knowledge was to what effect about the use of those helicopters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was aware, right from the start of my job, that the helicopters were flying in and out of Bosnia with or without guaranteed passage, as booked by them through ourselves, ECMM, to the U.N., to allow them safe passage. They were going with permission and without permission. Of that that I know, because I was the airfield monitor in Split. And on many occasions I'd sit waiting for them to come back and they were very late. Then I would get reports that they had been seen flying over middle Bosnia, doing things that they hadn't booked to do. In other words, they were dropping off parachuters and other bits of equipment. So I knew that they were applying for these medical evacuations to be known as Medivacs. And it transpired at a later stage that these Medivacs were actually allowing them to do other things under the guise of a Medivac. I was always very suspicious of what they were doing, but having moved into middle Bosnia in December, or November of '93, it didn't take very long to realise that they were actually using their helicopters for other things, for troop movements, and movement of staff in and out of the Nova Bila hospital in the Vitez pocket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As to the particular personalities you've already spoken of -- I am going to pause, because I've broken my rule about the interpreters. As to particular personalities you've spoken of, was anything said about them and their use of helicopters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was again common knowledge, and often referred to in conversation, that Mr. Kordic was using the helicopters, was being transported around in the helicopters to meet other members of the Herceg-Bosnia regime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose helicopters were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They belonged to both the HV, who were using the helicopters from -- based in basa Divulje, where my other team of airfield monitors are based, and also the HVO, whose base was in Posusje, not far from Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever speak to pilots of any of those helicopters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Before I came to Zenica, I spent a lot of time with the pilots, because it was my daily work to liaise with them. And I flew with them on a few occasions, but not right into middle Bosnia, just to the periphery. I never asked them who they were flying exactly, because at that point I hadn't quite worked it out. And by the time I realised what was going on, they were down in Split and I was in Zenica. But I can come on to an incident at a later time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'll deal with paragraphs 10 to 15 in their right chronological position, and turn to paragraph 16. Was there fighting in Santici, of which you became aware in January 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I went on leave back to the U.K. in December of '93. And when I came back, I was aware that heavy fighting had broken out in the Santici area, and actually, I was unable to make my way back to Zenica on the day of my return from leave, because the main supply route that went through Santici was blocked because of fighting that had broken out and had been led by the army of BiH, 3rd Brigade, and Croats were trying to defend that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there alleged Mujahedin involvement? Did you verify it? And what happened to the fleeing Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was aware of Mujahedin involvement within the whole area. I had seen them myself. I had run across them a few times. And during the fighting in Santici, one of the interpreters, who was working in Zenica, actually recognised one of the so-called Mujahedin. He had been at school with him. He was Muslim too. They were the spearhead, so-called spearhead of any BiH movement across middle Bosnia. They weren't backed by General Alagic. He had no respect for them and was quite keen for them to go. And when they attacked Santici, the Croat families were forced to flee to -- mostly to Zenica, to Father Stephan, who was the leader of the Croat church in Zenica, who I've since spoken to on a few occasions. I went to Zenica to find out where the families were, to check to see that they had food and clothing, and to do a head count. And I was also aware of at least two members of the Santici population that didn't manage to flee. I was witness to their bodies, and they were my first war crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've used the word "Mujahedin," but perhaps it would be helpful for you to give us your definition or the way you use that word.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before I came to the Vitez pocket, I had no idea what a Mujahedin looked like or even what his beliefs, if any, were. While I was in the Vitez pocket, I took it upon myself to read the Koran; not a riveting read, but it actually gives you an insight into what they believe. And the whole concept of Mujahedin in Bosnia, or be it anywhere else, is the war of El Jahid, and when I came across Mujahedin dead bodies, I realised that they had no regard for anybody else's life, not even their own. They waged a war of wanton destruction in the area. They didn't care who they dealt with en route. As I say, they had no regard for themselves. I know that the Croats were absolutely terrified of them, and so was I.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So are you using the term to define where somebody comes from or are you using the term to define somebody according to what he has done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm using the term "Mujahedin" because that's how they were referred to by the army of BiH leader in that area, Mehmet Alagic. He described them as such. There were two brigades of Mujahedin, one based in Travnik itself, which I believe, without checking from my notes, is the 37th Brigade, which were not so fundamentalist in their beliefs as 7th Mountain Brigade, who were based behind Guca Gora monastery. They were not locals. They were fairly dark-skinned and looked like they had come from some parts of Africa. They didn't speak the local language very well, and they moved together and were protected by various imams in and around the area. I knew them to be Mujahedin only because of their distinguishing features and because the Croats and the Muslims referred to them as such.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We can turn to paragraph 17 to 20, which I'm told I can lead on, and therefore, Witness Z, we can deal with this specifically or comparatively swiftly. On the 6th of January, 1994, did you visit a mass grave in Dubravica which the HVO said was the result of Bosnian Muslim atrocities, the claim being that there were 27 bodies in the grave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Restrictions of time and the fact that you were in a fragile ceasefire and, therefore, a dangerous place, meant that only eight bodies could be exhumed, all male, all apparently of fighting age and clad in military clothing, at least to the extent of one item of clothing per body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The bodies were in a state of decay; probably about a month, not even that. They had been buried in the garbage pit just outside of Poculica, which was a typical dumping area for dead bodies. We went with a British Battalion commander or a section commander, and we were right in the middle of the ceasefire between -- on BiH territory. It wasn't a comfortable area to stay, but I can confirm that I stood and watched at least eight bodies being dug up. They had all been bagged and tagged with a number beforehand by the British, and this was just us checking to make sure that they were -- hadn't been tortured, that they had just suffered gunshot wounds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you found nothing on those particular eight bodies to suggest that they had died other than as war casualties, and therefore nothing to confirm the HVO's allegations of BiH atrocities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. With these bodies, I found absolutely no reason to lead me to think that they had been tortured, as alleged by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And following that exercise, did your ECMM team set up a body exchange between the HVO and the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, we did, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in mid-January '94, did General Alagic of the ABiH call you to investigate information that he had been given about five of his soldiers being tortured in HVO trenches, as a result of which you inspected five bodies shown by the HVO in a disused school in Vitez with two other people, a Captain York and Fred Schroeder, you then being told by Nikica Petrovic of the HVO that the identity card would be placed on the bodies concerned in order to identify the victims, but you similarly found on this side that they had gunshot wounds to the head, it being difficult to identify faces, and you were dependent on Petrovic's word that the identity cards and the bodies connected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. I went on the Friday to go and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If it's correct and it doesn't need amplification, because I'm able to lead this evidence, we can deal with this in that way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I miss something important, amplify. Otherwise, for this and the next paragraph, just acknowledge the accuracy. It wasn't possible to get a pathologist, and your colleagues concluded that the gunshot wounds were not unusual in time of war and that there was no sign of torture. This was explained to General Alagic, and he then agreed to participate in a body exchange?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That exchange was organised for the 1st of February of '94?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were told that the bodies produced by the BiH had been tortured, as he suspected, and did you view those bodies at the mosque in Poculica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I answer that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Alagic was claiming that the bodies had actually been tortured, but when I had seen them prior to the body swap, the bodies that I had been shown were not tortured. Three days later, on the 4th of February, when I went to Poculica, to the mosque, I was shown five very badly-tortured bodies. They weren't the ones that I had been shown in the school. The reason I went to Poculica is because that's where they came from. They were being delivered back to the families.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So by whom had you been misled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Croats had misled me on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By producing to you bodies that showed no torture, although on exchange it was discovered that they were -- the ones produced on exchange were tortured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, of course, you had only been in a position to see eight of the alleged 27 bodies, if it was 27 bodies in the mass grave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were 27 bodies in the mass grave, because come the day of the body swap on the 1st of February, I was able to see all of them lying on the ground. But because we had the television cameras for this from the BBC, and because it was an exceptionally cold day, and because I was standing between the lines of the army of BiH and the HVO, who had already shot at me earlier, I wasn't really going to hang around. So we did the body swap as quickly as possible. On reflection, I think I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you attempt to investigate these deaths over the following weeks, but what was Petrovic's attitude and what was Alagic's attitude?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it's relevant to say here that Alagic tasked me to go and see these five bodies before the swap because he had been notified from a family based in Poculica that they had actually seen these five bodies being paraded on Croatian television, which because of the proximity and it was so close to Poculica, people in Poculica were able to pick up the TV up there, higher up in the valley, and they had actually seen these chaps being paraded. So I spent the next five weeks asking anybody that would talk to me about the allegations. I even went to the Hotel Vitez to see the TV producer who was working for Martin Bell at the time to ask him for footage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any success?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the ultimate attitude of Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Petrovic said, "At least Alagic got his bodies back." I knew at that point I was going to get nowhere. I had spent five weeks, and I wasn't prepared to waste any more time on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are small bundles of documentary exhibits which are in chronological order. If they can be distributed now, including one set to the witness. The documents, may they please be under seal? They needn't go on the ELMO for the usual reasons. We'll be turning to them only briefly. If the witness can have them herself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 10. You did meet Kordic. Tell us about the first meeting and when it happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I first met Mr. Kordic on the 16th of February in what was described as his Daca in Busovaca. I went there with my boss, Mr. William Stutt, my interpreter, and I went to visit him because I had been directed to go and visit him or have an interview with him in regard to a case that I was handling. I made an appointment, and I went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we look at the documents that have been placed before you, the first one, 1362,1, the second, 1364,2, and the third, 1375,1, deal with the matters we've just covered about the dead bodies. But since it's been possible to lead that information as unchallenged, although the documents can be produced, we needn't deal with them in detail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so we come to your first meeting on the 16th of February of 1994, and that is the next exhibit, 1377, the second sheet of it and, indeed, the last substantive paragraph. The topic of your meeting at his Daca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wanted to meet Mr. Kordic because I was trying to move the imam of Busovaca away from Busovaca. I had been given him as a case, and I had visited him on several occasions. He was hungry, his family were being intimidated, and he was under so-called house arrest. The imam was very frightened and very concerned about members of his family who had been intimidated, bullied, harassed, verbally abused. He had had his mosque blown up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He wanted to leave the area. I asked Mr. Kordic, when it was my turn to speak, if he would grant me passage to remove the imam from Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A few questions. Deal with them all compendiously but briefly. When he received you, was he alone or with others, what was his manner, and then tell us what he said about the imam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I arrived at the so-called Daca in Busovaca, I was met by six or seven men with short hair and pale green uniforms on, pale green uniforms. They had AK-47s and pistols on their body. They moved myself and Mr. Stutt out of the vehicle in a hurried manner and moved me inside, where I was introduced to Mr. Kordic. His manner was rather menacing and that of a bully, and I did feel intimidated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His response or attitude to the particular problem of the imam when, as you said, it was your turn to speak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very offhand and almost laughing at my request, as if I had just asked the stupidest question. He was not going to help me with my request, and he went on to explain why not, which didn't make much sense, and I was rather dismissed out of hand. But I wasn't going to be put down, so I went at him again. In the end, he said that he'd think about it but that he was a pragmatist and that he didn't see why he should honour my request.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We see this meeting summarised in the second sheet of 1377 under the paragraph beginning: "During a visit to Dario Kordic ..." We turn on from that meeting. The next document, 1378,1, which reflects the same meeting, is that right, at Item 4(VI), or is this another meeting on the following day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. 1378,1 refers to me going to see the imam the following day to give him the results of my meeting with Mr. Kordic, because I promised the imam that I would go and see Mr. Kordic on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the impasse remained. The imam reiterated his request?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologised to the imam and told him that I wasn't here to move him and his family. And he was very sad about that, but I told him to hang on because I hadn't given up at that point and that I was going to see Mr. Kordic again as soon as he was back in the pocket and as soon as I had the time to go and see him. In fact --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next document is 1381,1 for the 19th of February, and it says simply that, under 4(VI), you arranged a meeting with Dario Kordic for Monday, the 21st of February?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was he at the time; did you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was just told by the liaison officers in the Hotel Vitez that Mr. Kordic was not currently in the pocket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by "pocket," does that refer to the overall pocket surrounded as it might have been or to some other more local area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sorry. The Vitez area of Busovaca-Vitez itself and the area towards Travnik, which was surrounded, as you quite rightly say, was known in those days as the Vitez pocket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that "out of pocket" meant that he had been able to travel, by some means, elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 1386,1 is the next document, and I think you can help us here with something about helicopters in some detail, but also you can deal perhaps with the visit to Mr. Kordic on the 21st of February. The 21st of February, do you have a note of that meeting or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't, no. I seem to have lost my notes, the 21st of February. But I have recorded it on -- I make reference to it on the 23rd of February, which is one of the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And putting things in order, did you visit him on the 21st of February, as we can see from the next following document, 1386,2, I think?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what had his attitude been on the 21st?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I visited him on the 16th, as I said, his mood was fairly menacing and fairly aggressive towards me. When I visited him again on the 21st, he was almost in a carnival mood. He was fairly joyous and fairly buoyant. I didn't quite know what was going on, but I was quite pleased to see a change in his manner. But he still didn't answer the question about the imam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that stage, were you able to work out why there was this apparent change?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had no idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In due course, you were able to put a reason to it, and we'll come to that in its sequence. But as you helpfully remind me, it's on your report of the 23rd of February, under, "2. Political Situation," that you hark back to Monday's meeting with Kordic and ECMM and UNPROFOR; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, then let's, having dealt with that meeting, come back to Document 1386,1 and to something that happened, I think, on the 22nd of February concerning a helicopter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would you like me to expand?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Part of my monitoring duties in the Vitez pocket was to visit both Croats and Muslims, which I tried to do with a great deal of impartiality. One of my areas was the Nova Bila church in the area of Nova Bila. The church had been turned into a field hospital, because Croats had no chance to use the facilities of a hospital in Vitez pocket. Both hospitals were outside. One was in Travnik and one was in Zenica. So they had to make do with what they could get. And they turned the church into a field hospital in Nova Bila. Because they were surrounded and because they were constantly under fire from snipers who were Muslims and Serbs from higher areas, the casualties in the Nova Bila field hospital were beyond my belief. A lot of the casualties were not always there, when I came back for a second visit. At first I had assumed that they had died. But when I got to know the priest that was running the Nova Bila hospital, a Franciscan priest, he told me they were actually being rotated out. When I asked him to expand about "rotating out," he said that helicopters would come in the night and pick up the casualties if they could pay to leave. Well, around about the 20th of February I was aware that my airfield monitors based in Split had been approached by a nurse from England called Sally Baker. It was her proposal to bully her way into Nova Bila to take out injured children from the Nova Bila hospital. But she was unable to get to them by road, because the fighting was so intense, and it was totally out of the question. I since found out, after my airfield monitors tipped me off, so to speak, that Sally Baker had actually flown in with the help of an MI8, which is a Russian-built helicopter, into the quarry at Vitez, a well-known landing site for these helicopters, and had achieved her aim of rescuing these children and had flown out again. And as a result of her arrival in the pocket, senior Croatian doctors had also arrived at the Nova Bila hospital. And I saw them. And I noticed that some of those children had in fact gone, and that some of the soldiers had in fact gone too. So I was aware of the fact that there was helicopter movement, and it was confirmed initially by this incident. That's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you aware of how Kordic had -- if he had been out of the pocket -- returned at about this time or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't physically see him return, or even depart. But the mere fact that these helicopters were operational, and the very fact that we couldn't use any of the roads for these known players, if you want to refer to them as such, there was actually only one way in and one way out. And, as I said, it was common knowledge by the locals, those that lived in the Vitez pocket, that the helicopter was the one, almost reliable, route in and out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next document, please, 1387,1, which is dated the 28th of February. The second sheet under "humanitarian activity" records your team's visit to the chief imam of Zenica. And comparative success there required a visit to be agreed with and then arrangements to be agreed by Kordic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. Mr. Kordic, I felt, in my first meeting, was only going to allow me to move the imam of Busovaca out, if he thought that he was going to let it happen, and if I had something to bargain with. So my bargaining tool was Father Stephan from Zenica, a Croat priest who I was going to bring in to the Vitez pocket so that he could visit his people on the ground on the Vitez pocket. And I would pull the imam of Busovaca from Vitez pocket to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your next meeting with Kordic was when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mid-March sometime. But it wasn't my meeting; I was just taking the notes at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us about it, in any event, even if you have to do so from -- substantially from memory.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We've moved on a bit now from February and the Federation has been signed, and the mood within the pocket and the army BiH has changed somewhat, but it seems that it's meeting with resistance from Mr. Kordic and from Mr. Alagic. And I went along to a meeting in Busovaca with my boss, with Martin Garrod, HCC of Zenica, ECMM, and Mr. Nick Turnbull, who I took over from back at the beginning of December. We tried to start talks with Mr. Kordic about the HVO involvement and demilitarisation within the Lasva Valley, and tried to bring in the BiH from Zenica, Travnik. Mr. Kordic didn't really want to get involved in any of these talks, and it was quite apparent that he was pulling the strings in the Vitez pocket. Everything had to go through him. And at that time, and I've written this down because I was taking the notes of this meeting, Mr. Kordic said that at this time the process for discussion had not yet arrived. That was that. End of discussion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you met him on this occasion. With whom on his side was he in company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had no political accomplices at that point. He was on his own. He had a plethora of men of military status? I described them as short-haired, fairly burly individuals, bristling with ammunition and rifles, and obviously acting as bodyguards, because they moved very close to Mr. Kordic whenever he stepped out of his room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In these discussions with comparatively senior or very senior people on your side, did he have to refer to anybody else before making decisions? Did he have to pick up the telephone or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The telephone links were rather sporadic at that time. We were actually in the Vitez pocket, rather cut off from the rest of middle Bosnia. But he did say that he wasn't prepared to make any high-level decisions without first discussing the questions with people of higher authority. And he never actually named anybody of higher authority, but he made reference to them in general.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did these attempted negotiations conclude?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you referring, sorry, to the ones in mid-March?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were non-conclusive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This meeting in mid-March, by what title, if any, did Kordic introduce himself, or identify himself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Self-proclaimed politician of Herceg-Bosnia for the Vitez pocket, and Colonel of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this the first time he'd called himself a Colonel in the HVO, or had it happened earlier, or can't you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's the first time that he referred to himself as a HVO Colonel. But I had heard him referred to as such by other people in and around the pocket that I had met in the course of my work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that your last meeting with Kordic, or were there later ones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For completeness, it's right that you saw Blaskic on various occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Starting when and finishing when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time I saw Commander Blaskic was on the television on the 3rd of January. And he was standing in front of the ammunition depot in Vitez pocket. And then I had two meetings with him at a later stage, January, February time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll deal with the television programme first. What was the content of what he was saying then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As you rightly pointed out a while ago, Vitez pocket was surrounded by troops of the army BiH, and Commander Blaskic, although he was the commander of middle Bosnia, he had wired the ammunition factory in Vitez with explosives. And he went on the television to provoke General Alagic, it would seem, and he threatened the Muslims at the time that if they tried to capture the Vitez pocket, he would blow up the ammunition dump. And he showed various monitors the ammunition dump and the wires and the explosive devices, the TNT that he described, although I never saw it; it was passed onto me. But I actually saw him on the television, the 3rd of January, standing in front of the ammunition dump. He was very tired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you spoke to Ivica Saric, former President of Travnik and the HVO President of the Exchange Commission, about this, or at least he commented on this, to the effect that fatigue was playing a part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Ivica Saric, former President of Travnik, displaced government of Travnik, shall we say, or displaced President of Travnik, was then hiding out in the -- well, not hiding out, but for his own safety living in the Hotel Vitez, or close to the Hotel Vitez. He was a very well-educated man, in my assumption. And he described Commander Blaskic as tired, exhausted. And the very fact that he had been on the television -- he described his showing on the television as irrational behaviour, due to his exhaustion, and trying to look after his people in the Vitez pocket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the two subsequent occasions that you saw Blaskic, what was he wearing by way of uniform and rank insignia, and what did he tell you, if anything, about rank insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On both occasions, Commander Blaskic was wearing what we in the army would describe as DPM clothing. That's disruptive pattern material, tree-suit material, green and brown. On his right arm he had a patch with HVO on it, which is Croatian army, and he had no badges of rank. They are normally now above the pockets, but he had nothing. And I asked him what rank he was. He said that it was too early for ranks, and that the Croatian army didn't have any ranks that were yet decided or given out. That would come at a later date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How, overall, did Kordic's attitude appear to you, contrasted, if it's appropriate, with Blaskic's?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Compared to Blaskic, his manner was pushy, unprofessional, menacing, intimidating, and that of a bully.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Professional, honest, when asked direct questions, keen to make sure that we didn't, as an ECMM team, take ourselves into any positions of danger. He was always looking out for our safety. And for that I was very grateful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Last two documents and two more questions, please. 1393,1. Now, you've told us about a Medivac or about Medivac helicopter problems. But this is now on the 11th of March. Just explain this, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said earlier, the only field hospital that we had in Nova Bila had a series of very sick patients, be they young or old. At this point, on around the 9th of March, I was contacted by the airfield monitors in Split and told to prepare for an arrival of MI8's from basa Divulje to the hospital in Nova Bila. So I got myself into position that day, the 11th of March --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's coming from the state of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Coming from the state of Croatia to the Republic of Bosnia. To my area, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time that the helicopters were due to arrive, I noticed them flying towards the hospital, but I noticed that they were dropping too quickly and that they actually weren't going to land where I was situated in my vehicle. I had no idea where they were going to land. So I followed the tail and found that they had actually landed in a school yard about one kilometre from where I was waiting in my vehicle. I got on the radio and I contacted the BritBat G5 officer, Captain York, who I had worked with on many occasions. And I asked him to get to the grid reference I quoted to him, because I suspected that something was about to go amiss. Within a very short period of time, Captain York arrived in his Land Rover, with the aid of one Warrior tank, APC, whatever you want to call it. And I noticed, because we had arrived in time to see the helicopter landing, and we noticed that coming out of the back of the MI8 were approximately 20 soldiers in new uniforms, carrying weapons, carrying bags, carrying boxes. The boxes -- some of the boxes were leaking oil. And from my military experience, I can only tell you that when boxes leak oil, there is something inside there, like explosives. Inside their bags, although we couldn't see them, we could hear ammunition chinking. And the soldiers were being greeted, by those who had gathered quickly, as a hero's welcome. I asked my interpreter to listen to what was being said. She said that these guys had apparently come from Gornji Vakuf, which was south from us. So I asked Captain York if he could get some more Warriors, and that we were going to surround the helicopter so that it couldn't fly off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Within a short period, two more Warriors came and trained their cannon on their -- on the MI8s. And then I recognised one of the pilots and I put him in my truck and took him to BritBat, because he wouldn't get in the BritBat truck. And I took him to the ops room in BritBat to meet the Colonel of BritBat, and also Commander Filipovic was there as well. This was the first time that I'd actually witnessed the MI8 landing in the Vitez pocket. This was now after the war and it was during the daylight hours, and it seemed to me as if they had become quite complacent. And they were doing this, knowing full well that I was going to be around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the flight from Croatia, cleared for Medivac purposes, apparently abused?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. The airfield monitors in Split had actually cleared the helicopter, as was the procedure, before it took off. By the time it arrived at Nova Bila, it was no longer empty. It was full of troops. And the troops had been picked up en route. We can't say exactly where, but we suspect that they were picked up from Poculica. Or not Poculica; from Posusje, I beg your pardon, which was the Croatian helicopter base in southern part of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that would again be coming from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It left Croatia empty. By the time it arrived with me it was full.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is dealt with in document 1393,1, where the query is raised. At number 2, are you able to confirm whether troops or passengers exited from the helicopter when it landed? And your report can be found at 1393,2. We notice at the foot of the first page, at the end of paragraph 1, that the Croatian television had recorded Mr. Kordic being back in Busovaca at that time, but then under 2, operational military matters, and over the page, the account of this helicopter incident, which you dealt with, is there set out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. Yes. You want me to expand?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you've covered everything that there is there. So far as you know, the soldiers were sent back, except that 19 went back and not 18?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, the 19 that I refer to there were actually --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am so sorry. Nineteen patients?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nineteen patients. I actually loaded 19 and not 18, because there was one more that I took pity on, and there was this space left in the seekings that came to pick up Croat people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the Medivac mission was completed with seeking helicopters and, so far as you know, the other helicopter did go back and, presumably, went back with the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shall I expand?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the helicopter that was grounded by force, shall I say, from the Warriors, was actually held on the ground. And Commander Filipovic insisted that all the soldiers that had actually got out from the helicopter be rounded up and taken back to where they came from. Now, this did happen, although I have no report to show it. They were picked up, and around about 6.00 that evening they were flown back. I had to be back in there each night at 5.00 to start my report and to meet the curfew time. But they did get flown back. But, as it happens, they didn't arrive in Split; they were dropped off in Posusje, where another 19 or 20 of them were loaded. And they were older guys. They weren't the same ones that were pulled out of the Vitez pocket. So when they arrived back in Split, where everybody was waiting for them, they weren't the ones that jumped out of the helicopter earlier that -- the day before. In other words, the game playing had still continued, even though they had been exposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If I can deal with paragraphs 22 and 23 before the adjournment, then I would have concluded the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How long is it going to take?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not very long, I don't think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 22, your translator who is named, but don't name her, did she tell you about an attack on her village of Dusina in January of 1993? Just "Yes" or "No."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And she gave an account of what happened to her and her brothers, which you summarised in the summary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you interviewed by someone named in paragraph 23 of your summary about the abduction of that person's husband?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was approached by her. I wasn't interviewed by her, but, yes --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You interviewed her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I interviewed her, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On many occasions. That was the first one in January.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was in relation to the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, I'm not going to take that further. I think that's all I want from this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn now. Witness Z, would you be back, please, at half past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.05 p.m. 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and good afternoon, Witness Z. My name is Steven Sayers. I am one of the attorneys representing Dario Kordic. We'll try to get through with your questions so that you can leave today. Ma'am, you gave a statement on February 11th and 12 of 1997 to Mr. Carry Spork, one of the Prosecution's investigators; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That consists of 13 pages, single spaced, and it is pretty detailed, chronologically. Did you consult any personal notes, any journals or contemporaneous diary that you kept before preparing that statement and giving it to the Prosecution's investigators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For certain aspects of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you have any contemporaneous notes made of the three conversations that you've related to the Trial Chamber concerning Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only notes that I have concerning Mr. Kordic are the ones that I wrote when I came back from my day out in the Vitez pocket, which was done on a daily basis around about half past 4.00, 5.00 each night. So I am referring to those notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You are referring to the notes which were subsequently typed up, and which were marked as exhibits and shown to you today, I take it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The notes that I have given as exhibits were actually written by myself at the time in 1994. Yes, they would have been done by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say, ma'am, that those notes, or the entries in the exhibits that we've seen today, represent the sum total of the material that you've actually written yourself about each of those three meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, the statement that you gave to Mr. Spork two and a half years ago, was that given in your words or were someone else's words used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were given by me, at my private accommodation, and taken down over the space of about three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It would be fair to say, I take it, that you signed that statement as an accurate representation of what you had personally told the investigator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I noticed, ma'am, that you have some facility with the pronunciation of Croatian names. Do you actually speak the Croatian language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Did you have that ability when you were performing your functions as an ECMM monitor between December of 1993 and July of 1994, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I first got to Croatia, I couldn't speak a word of language. I've learnt it since I have been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not fluent, but I am working on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The fact is, though, that at the end of 1993, and in early 1994, you actually needed the services of an interpreter to be able to converse with people on the ground; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just a few background questions, ma'am, to make sure I've got the chronological facts straight. I understand that your first mission to the former Yugoslavia was from August to November, and that you spent that time actually in the Republic of Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, my first mission was for a year, but I spent the first part of my mission as an airfield monitor based in Croatia, yes, that's correct, from August until November.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You came to Zenica for the first time on November the 5th of 1993, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right. I had actually taken a growing interest in what was going on in the area, and because -- I suppose because of my interests and because of my background, I was asked if I would like to take over the team working in Vitez. But it was pointed out to me that I would be the only female around and that it was actually a fairly difficult area in which to work. And I was asked whether I would like to take over the job, to which I said yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You were asked some questions right at the end of your direct examination about the events at Dusina in January of 1993. I would just like to ask you a few questions in that regard. But I think, Mr. President, we may have to go into private session to do so, with the Trial Chamber's permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You are asking to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, ma'am. Just a couple of very general questions regarding the HVO chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You understood that the general staff of the HVO, the military forces, was located in Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you also understood that the supreme commander of the armed forces was actually the president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, a man by the name of Mate Boban; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes, but I also understood that his supreme commander was President of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did he ever tell you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Did who ever tell me that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Boban?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never met Mr. Boban. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And when you were present in Central Bosnia, ma'am, do you know who the chief of the general staff of the HVO was, who the military commander was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was told and introduced to Commander Blaskic as such, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me suggest to you, ma'am, that Commander Blaskic was the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, or the 3rd Operative Zone at that time, and that he reported to a superior officer who, while you were present in Central Bosnia, was General Ante Rosso. Does that name mean anything to you at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rosso, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And on the subject of Commander Blaskic, you had no doubt that he was, in fact, the commander of all of the HVO military forces within his area of responsibility; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And when issues such as the unfortunate issue of body exchanges or exchanges of wounded arose, you naturally contacted the military authorities to arrange that; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, it was pretty much the other way around. They always had firsthand knowledge of when it was right to go ahead with those things, and I was to report to them on a daily basis, which I did sort of in the course of my work, and they would update me. I used to go to the Hotel Vitez every day to go and talk with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You gave some testimony, ma'am, regarding what Colonel Blaskic told you in connection with the HVO rank system, if you like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I would just like to show you a document and ask you whether you ever had the opportunity to see this at any time or hear about it while you were on your tour of duty.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D140/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This document was published in something known as the Narodni List of HZ Herceg-Bosna. Had you ever heard of that gazette before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand it's a people's list of Herceg-Bosna. No, I've never seen this document before. It's the first time I see it today. I see it's signed by Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right, on July the 3rd of 1992. But if you've never seen it before, ma'am, there appears to be little point in asking you any questions on it, so let's move on. Did you ever have the opportunity to meet a gentleman by the name of Dr. Jadranko Prlic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you know that Dr. Prlic was actually the President of the HVO before the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was formed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever have the opportunity, ma'am, to speak to any of the three vice-presidents of the HVO: Mr. Stipo Ivankovic, Mr. Kresimir Zubak or Mr. Anto Valenta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know the names. I have never met the gentlemen in question, no. I know that Mr. Zubak is a political figure in Croatia, because I saw posters of him two years ago, during the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were you aware that Mr. Zubak had actually signed the Washington Agreement that terminated hostilities on March the 1st of 1994, and he signed in his capacity as representative of the Croat people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, obviously?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, end of February, 1994. Around about the 25th of February. Around about that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I can make this an exhibit or not, as the case may be. Let me just represent to you that according to a letter dated March the 3rd of 1994, from the permanent representatives of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia to the United Nations and to the Secretary-General, there is a reference to two documents signed in Washington on the 1st of March 1994, which are known as the Washington Agreements.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Signed by Mr. Haris Silajdzic, the Prime Minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Granic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Granic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And Mr. Kresimir Zubak, head of the Bosnian Croat delegation. Does that refresh your memory as to the precise date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It does, because the ceasefire was called for 12.00 on the 25th of February, so that was the natural conclusion that followed on, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you follow the genesis of this so-called Stoltenberg Owen plan at all, ma'am, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't understand it, to be perfectly honest. I understood what they were attempting to do, but I think it was -- my own opinion -- premature and incredibly optimistic. And it only took two sides into account. It totally ruled out the third element. So it was a non-starter, as far as we could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Was that a view that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Mr. Sayers, could the witness tell us more precisely what she was referring to, the two first elements and the third element?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The third element being the Serb element. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the first two elements, therefore, are the Croats and the Muslims? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. I didn't get all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me try to clear this up. With the permission of the Trial Chamber, I do not believe that a copy of the Stoltenberg Owen plan has ever been made an exhibit, and it might be helpful just to ask a few questions of that by way of background to clarify for everybody what the proposal was. This is a relatively substantial document, Your Honour. But I would only wish to point out three separate paragraphs in it. And I think that you can see what the International Community was attempting to achieve. Thanks. If we could have this marked as the next Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There is no need to go through this fairly weighty document in any detail, ma'am. I would just like to point out to you certain salient features. If you just turn to page 5 of the document, paragraph 19. There is a reference here to the fact that, after intensive discussions of a number of drafts, all three parties agreed, on the 30th of July, 1993, to a constitutional agreement for a Union of Republics of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and to that Union forming part of an overall peace settlement. The next page, the paragraph I would like to draw your attention to, is on the next page, paragraph 24, where all three sides agree that the name of each constituent republic would be determined by the competent authorities of that republic. Was that your understanding of one facet of the agreement, ma'am, or does that not ring even a faintly familiar bell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It rings bells, but what's written here on paper wasn't actually what was being thought out at the time. And I say that purely because the only two sides that you could get to talk to were indeed the army BiH and the HVO. There was no -- for us, as ECMM monitors, there was no even -- no thought of talking with the third side. And, in fact, they didn't even sign the agreement, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And, in fact, even though that dialogue was going on, it was not eased by the fact that there was a major, widespread offensive being mounted by the ABiH in the summer of 1993 against HVO forces. And, if you want to, take a look at paragraph 37 on page 9. A reference is made to that. Did you have any personal knowledge or knowledge from your colleagues at the ECMM regarding that ABiH offensive in the summer of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't there in 1993, in the summer, I'm afraid. I can't comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: My final question. If you just turn to page 13, appendix 1, which articulates the constitutional agreement of the Union of Republics of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There were to be three constituent republics which encompass the three constituent peoples: Muslims, Serbs and Croats. Is that a fair synopsis of what the Stoltenberg Owen Plan was intended to achieve, in your recollection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On paper, yes. In reality, not a chance. As I say, it was a bit optimistic, a bit too -- it's a good idea, but it was ahead of its time. Unfortunately, it didn't work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Ma'am, there is no question, though, that the Croats accepted this plan and agreed to abide by it; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Stoltenberg agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Stoltenberg agreement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't say for sure exactly what they had in their mind, but it would probably ring true, because at a later stage they signed up to the Federation, in March '94.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And shortly after this agreement was signed or approved by the Croat side, do you recall that the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was actually founded in Mostar on the 28th of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I have a document, not with me, but it was signed by Mate Boban on the 5th of August, 1992, where he declares himself as the President of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna. So we missed a year here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me show you one other document, ma'am. It may or may not help refresh your memory as to this topic. But it's actually the founding document of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. I believe I may have misspoken somewhat, ma'am, when I said the republic was founded in Mostar. It was actually founded in Grude on that day. Could you just turn to the second page, ma'am. You can see that this document was signed by the President of the House of Representatives, Perica Jukic. Did you ever meet that gentleman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Does his name ring a familiar bell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I know nothing about the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Now, did you realise, ma'am, that the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna ceased to exist once the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was founded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, will you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you realise that the Croatian community, an entity known as the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, the so-called HZHB, ceased to exist once the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Okay. Just a few questions, ma'am, if I may, regarding Mr. Kordic. In your statement two and a half years ago, you made the observation that the precise nature of Mr. Kordic's position in this republic was uncertain after the political exit of Mr. Mate Boban. You made that observation on page 8. Would it be fair to say that there was a considerable degree of uncertainty within the ECMM regarding the nature of Mr. Kordic's offices, if any, in the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be fair to say so, yes. It would also be fair to say that you couldn't get a straight answer, so you were left to try and find out the answers any way you could. These were not particularly clear times, as I'm sure you realise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The ECMM, though, actually had available to it the decrees of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, such as those which appointed members of the government; did it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HCC would have had access to this, because he attended high-level meetings. They would have been passed down, but, to be perfectly honest, I never saw them. I was going on verbal instructions. And my job was to go out there and confirm what was either being passed around as a rumour or that that was written down. I was gathering information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So even though the documents that articulated the appointments of members of the government were available to the head of a regional centre, the HRC, the position is that you yourself never actually saw them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sad to say, but that's the truth, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Then we can move on. A number of references to Mr. Kordic and inquiries about his position appear, ma'am, in the records of the ECMM. I'd just like to show you a few, if I may. The first one is dated the 15th of December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Written by Mr. Turnbull, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just checking, and I'll let you know. The authors of this document appear to be a gentleman by the name of Aage Terp, Gerard van der Elshout, and Johan Swennen. Let me just show it to you, if I may.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I know all three of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Just --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The last document was marked D142/1, and this document is marked D143/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just two or three questions about this document, ma'am. There's a reference to the HCC in Mostar meeting a gentleman called Slobodan Lovrenovic, who is the press advisor to Mate Boban. When asked specifically about the status of Mr. Kordic, who had been a vice-president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the HCC was informed that Mr. Kordic no longer held presidential office but merely was one of many legislators in the house of representatives. Do you recall any internal discussion at the ECMM in December or January on this topic, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Similarly, at the bottom of the page, there's a reference to a discussion between the HCC of Travnik, who I gather was Mr. Stutt --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- a discussion between him and Mr. Blaskic, and the topic of Mr. Kordic's status within the republic cropped up, and Colonel Blaskic informed Mr. Stutt that he was not a politician and had not followed the political process. Did you have any discussion on that subject about Mr. Kordic's status with Mr. Stutt at around this time, ma'am, or shortly thereafter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Stutt is a military man, and it's a well-known fact that military and politicians don't mix terribly well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That he says -- that Mr. Blaskic says that he doesn't know anything about politics comes as no surprise. I think I'd give the same answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The next ECMM report, I don't need to go into that. Let me just see if I can pick up the pace here a little, ma'am. On the subject of helicopter flights about which you testified, you never actually saw Mr. Kordic take a flight in a helicopter at any time after you took up your duties as a V1 ECMM monitor in December of 1993, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And I believe that the only helicopter landing that you witnessed yourself, the one in which the Warriors apprehended it by force, occurred after the war had already ended, after the signature of the Washington Agreements.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the one that I actually witnessed. I saw them leaving from Split before. We had had a lot of reported helicopter movement which was taking place during the night during the war, which made sense; they were hardly going to fly during the day. But the only one that I did see was the one that actually landed on the 11th of March, I believe it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: After the signature of the Washington --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct. Still a violation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: One question, if I may, about the subject that you gave regarding the imam in Busovaca. In your statement two and a half years ago, you made no reference to the imam, did you? I mean you have reviewed your statement, I take it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To be honest, I would have to check my statement again about the imam, but I can't say off the top of my head because I haven't got the document here in front of me, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. If I might just show you the next document I would like to have marked, which is an ECMM report from the CC Travnik, February 16, 1994. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D144/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The CC Travnik, as we've established, is Mr. Stutt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And he was the one that actually drafted the political situation summary that is contained on page 1; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe I was sitting right next to him when he did it. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Would it be fair to say that Mr. Stutt was doing most of the talking and you were actually taking notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it's not true, actually; not on this particular occasion, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You came out and spoke your mind on that one particular subject; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was my meeting. I took Mr. Stutt along for protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And that was the first meeting that you had had with Mr. Kordic, as we've established; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
