utterances.text: Now, did the imam tell you that he had actually been paying visits to his mother and spending time in Kacuni?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember him saying that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If he did, he must have done it before my time, because by the time I got to him, he was going -- he wasn't allowed out of the house. But Kacuni at that time was cut off, so there was only one route into Kacuni and that was -- I interviewed one gentleman that had gone from Travnik to Kacuni, and it took him 12 hours, with the aid of a donkey. So I don't know how the imam got to Kacuni. He must have done it before I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. It's true, ma'am, that while you were in Central Bosnia, the ABiH launched two large offensives in the Vitez-Busovaca area; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The first was just before Christmas on December the 22nd and the 24th, 1993, and that resulted in numerous deaths and casualties, an attack on Krizancevo Selo, and it was those bodies that you saw exhumed about a month later, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And then the second attack was on Santici and Buhine Kuce, I believe-- please forgive my pronunciation -- on the 9th of January, 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, ma'am, that between those two events, those two offensives, the ECMM's view was that morale in the Vitez-Busovaca pocket, at least from the Croat perspective, was as low as anybody could remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, let me just go back a step here. Do you mean that the morale of the HVO soldiers was low?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the civilians, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think they had gone into survival mode, if you ask my opinion. It wasn't as low as the army of BiH, but it wasn't far off it. They were struggling, both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I don't think we need to make this an exhibit, but from the RC Zenica daily report for December the 28th, 1993, the head of the regional centre makes the observation that HVO morale in Vitez, Kiseljak, and Zepce is as low as anybody can recall having seen it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 28th of December, 1993, I was actually away in the U.K. on leave, so if he says that's the case, then that must have been based on the previous Victor 1 leader who I took over from, so presumably that's the conclusion that they came to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And that was Mr. Turnbull?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The testimony that you gave regarding threats made by Commander Blaskic to explode the SPS factory in Vitez, those warnings were fairly routine, weren't they? They had been going on for a number of months and it was really nothing new?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's what I could describe as normal Balkan provocation. It seems threatening to us, but it's normal life where they live. I thought it was quite a good plan myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: A few questions, ma'am, on the subject of the ABiH attack on Santici on the 9th of January, 1994. There's no question that this was a concerted 3rd Corps assault on the main supply route at Santici, spearheaded by Mujahedin forces; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The Mujahedin forces, in fact, were supplemented by troops from the 3rd Corps, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And in launching the attacks on the village of Santici, the assault troops used standard FIBUA tactics, fighting in built-up area tactics, standard house-to-house clearance tactics, as far as you could see; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the army of BiH troops used those type of tactics? I didn't see them do it, but if they did, they made a fairly poor stab at it, because I've seen it done professionally and it was not very well done. In fact, it was just haphazard and fairly sporadic, with a hint of optimistic attached. They didn't get very far.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All of the Bosnian Croat civilians who declined to flee from their homes, though, were killed, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw two casualties, two dead bodies from the attack on Santici, yes. They were -- one was unable to run away because he had been hit by a car a year earlier and he was on crutches. They grabbed him first. There was a female of about 35 years old. She was lying dead in the garden in the same area. I know of two that couldn't leave the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 5 of your statement, you said that you saw two women shot dead in their garden as they were trying to escape the assault. Is that consistent with your current recollection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw one woman in the morgue and I saw one man who had been impaled. I don't remember the other woman, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. The second individual that you identified was about 60-years old, a crippled man who was killed and cut in half; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Umm-hmm, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That gentleman's -- the top half of his body was then impaled on a pole about nine or ten feet long; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know if anything was done within the 3rd Corps, ma'am, to investigate these appalling crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether any measures at all were taken to discipline or remove any military commanders who were responsible for that attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I asked General Mehmet Alagic about this, and he said it was the work of the Mujahedin. He said that the Mujahedin didn't come under his control from Cesko [phoen] Brigada. He said that they were working independently. And it transpired later that any dealings with the so-called Mujahedin were well and truly out of Alagic's reach. So although he was the commander, or second in commander, and then took over 7th Muslim Brigade, he actually didn't wield much power, because when I put him to the test, he couldn't help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I have a photograph here, ma'am. I would just like you to identify whether this was the gentleman that you saw in his dismembered condition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's him.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document marked D145/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: A very brief question, ma'am, on one of the exhibits that you were shown, Exhibit Z1381,1. There is a reference in this document to the Hotel Vitez, the HVO headquarters, being subjected to sporadic mortar fire from Stari Vitez. Was that a fairly common occurrence, in your view, during this war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Almost daily. In fact, the day that I went to see this exhibit here, they were busy shelling the Hotel Vitez every 40 minutes. I worked it out. And within those 40 minutes, I managed to run from the Hotel Vitez, to go and see this exhibit, and run back again. It was fairly intense, and it was going on every day, just about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just one question, ma'am, in connection with the mid-March 1994 meeting that you had with Mr. Kordic and your boss, if you like, Mr. Stutt.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That was after the Washington Agreement had already been signed, I take it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you know that Mr. Kordic had been appointed as the President of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna Commission for the implementation of the Washington Agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't. To be honest, I didn't at that time, no. I took notes that day. That wasn't my meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you have those notes with you, or are they lost?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have them here. Just give me a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Is there anything of a personal nature in there, or is it all business?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just have to check and make sure I haven't already submitted this one. Just give me a second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, you've now been nearly an hour on this cross-examination. How much longer do you require?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Perhaps five, ten minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Kovacic, are you cross-examining this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we don't.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't find it. It's in here somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's quite all right, ma'am. Just a few final questions on some final topics, if I may. First, you never saw, at any time during your tour of duty in Central Bosnia, detainees being used to dig trenches, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Or being used as so-called human shields?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I went to the prison in -- I can't pronounce it -- Kaonik, I think. It's near Busovaca anyway. And I saw what they had in there, but they weren't being used. But they were being accused of doing it. I never saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You yourself, though, never saw any people used for forced labour, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you never witnessed any maltreatment of detainees at any time during your tour; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You were asked some questions, ma'am, in connection with one topic that actually may require us to go into private session again, Mr. President, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: (Open Session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Madam Witness, would you state your --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would you speak into the microphone and state it, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you give us your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: NASIHA NESLANOVIC
utterances.text: Nasiha Neslanovic. I was born on the 16th of June, 1958, in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You were born in Busovaca and continued to live there until the war?

utterances.speaker: NASIHA NESLANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And your occupation formerly was mail courier and cleaning lady?

utterances.speaker: NASIHA NESLANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And you are, by ethnicity, a Bosniak or a person of the Muslim persuasion?

utterances.speaker: NASIHA NESLANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you work in Busovaca during the entire period up until the war?

utterances.speaker: NASIHA NESLANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Where did --

utterances.speaker: NASIHA NESLANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: -- you work?

utterances.speaker: NASIHA NESLANOVIC
utterances.text: In the municipal hall, in the municipal hall in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you know Dario Kordic when you lived in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: NASIHA NESLANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How long did you know him?

utterances.speaker: NASIHA NESLANOVIC
utterances.text: I knew him for a very long time, ever since we were children until this day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you have a professional relationship with Dario Kordic's mother?

utterances.speaker: NASIHA NESLANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because his mother was a physician. She treated my brother, myself, my child, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Where did you have treatment given by Dr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: NASIHA NESLANOVIC
utterances.text: The treatment was given in the health centre, and at times I also went to their home, that is, to their flat, if there was something urgent, if I needed some urgent care for my child or my brother or somebody. So we would go to her home for either some findings or for a prescription, whatever kind of help we needed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask the usher to show Z1472,1 to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you ever have treatment by Dr. Kordic after the war had begun in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: NASIHA NESLANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And where was the treatment given?

utterances.speaker: NASIHA NESLANOVIC
utterances.text: At the health centre in Busovaca. She treated me during the war because it was during the war I fell ill, and I went to the health centre and I was standing in the passage, and there was some military and civilians --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just tell us the doctor who treated you during the war. That's sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you simply tell us, is this the same Dom Zdravlja that is mentioned at the bottom of the page of the document that you have in front of you?

utterances.speaker: NASIHA NESLANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was there also a war hospital near Dom Zdravlja in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: NASIHA NESLANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a kindergarten which was then converted into a war hospital during the war. That is, they evacuated the children and turned it into a war hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And the time frame when you received your treatment from Dr. Kordic during the war, was it after 25th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: NASIHA NESLANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: At the time you were treated by Dr. Kordic, did she have on a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: NASIHA NESLANOVIC
utterances.text: No. She wore the professional white clothes, the white frock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, you referred to a Document 1472,1. We were handed a number of documents, but that one doesn't seem to be amongst them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry, Your Honour. It should have been a top document, actually, a separate one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have 175,1.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If it's not there, please give my copy. I apologise. It should have been in a pile with two copies.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This document is the announcement, is it, of an award to Dr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Appears to be.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I have no further questions of the document. I was identifying locations and whether or not there was a uniform at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Going back a bit in time, did something unusual happen on the steps of the police station in May of 1992 in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: NASIHA NESLANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was carrying the mail to the police station in Busovaca, there were some letters, and as I reached the stairs, I saw two men in black clothes. I first -- I thought they were chimney sweepers. But when I reached the staircase, I saw the two were wearing black uniforms with caps with the letter "U" on them, and I stopped at the staircase because I was very taken aback by this uniform. To my mind, it only existed in history in the past. I saw it in textbooks but never in reality. So I was rather lost, and one of the policemen took me by the hand so I could leave the mail there. Then I came back to the municipal hall very surprised and told my boss that I had seen those uniforms and with the letter "U". He said, "Well, this won't be the first time you're coming across that."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What did the letter "U" represent to you?

utterances.speaker: NASIHA NESLANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we learned about that in our history classes, that that meant -- that was the symbol of the Ustasha, that those were uniforms in the last war and those uniforms were rather old, and because -- they were pretty frayed and moth-eaten because they must have been concealed somewhere, lying somewhere for so many years. I mean, it was obvious that they could be dated to the last war, because they were very old. I mean those were really old clothes, really.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you recognise --

utterances.speaker: NASIHA NESLANOVIC
utterances.text: Quite old.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Did you recognise either of the persons wearing those uniforms?

utterances.speaker: NASIHA NESLANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recognised one of them. His last name was Marinic. I knew him. I believe he was Zoran Marinic's uncle, whom I used to know because he was a neighbour of mine and a friend too, and he lived not far from where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Does Zoran Marinic use any other name?

utterances.speaker: NASIHA NESLANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He was called Svabo. More people knew him as Svabo than by his real name and surname.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The boss to whom you addressed your concern, what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: NASIHA NESLANOVIC
utterances.text: He was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Going back a bit further yet, in November 1991 do you recall any referendum that was presented to you, as a citizen of Busovaca, to create or to vote to create the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: NASIHA NESLANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that. I never went out to such a referendum, nor do I know that there was one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In November '91, did you observe any changes in the way things were taking place around you in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: NASIHA NESLANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand. Oh, I see, yes. Yes, there were major changes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment. You know, Ms. Somers, we've heard quite a lot of evidence about this, so I think you can move on to the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It's okay. Thank you, Ms. Neslanovic. We'll move on to another question. Are you aware of what position, if any, Dario Kordic may have held in Busovaca through the HDZ after the 1991 elections?

utterances.speaker: NASIHA NESLANOVIC
utterances.text: Dario Kordic was appointed the chief of all national defence. He was designated to the post by the HDZ, and so he was the chief of the national defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: During that time period, did you see Dario Kordic during the course of the workday?

utterances.speaker: NASIHA NESLANOVIC
utterances.text: Practically every day. I mean, we met in the passage, in the corridor, every day. He came to work every day after he was appointed the head, the chief, for the national defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you involved in any work concerning his office? Did you have to go into his office?

utterances.speaker: NASIHA NESLANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: NASIHA NESLANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, to bring in whatever mail there would be, or to clean the place, or anything, or if I had to call somebody out who was there. So I mean I always went in on business, only when there was something official that had to be done; to take in letters, to sweep the office, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: During that time period, did you observe how Dario Kordic was dressed when he came to work?

utterances.speaker: NASIHA NESLANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the outset, he wore a civilian uniform, and then he would wear a military uniform too, that is, the multi-coloured -- the camouflage uniform. And that was as of April. As of April, people began to don camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: April of what year?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did he carry any weapons when he came to work, that you could see?

utterances.speaker: NASIHA NESLANOVIC
utterances.text: From time to time, yes. Now and then; not always. But I would see him. Sometimes he would have a pistol over his clothes, and sometimes he would take off his jacket and then we would see the pistol. That was his personal weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did he have bodyguards?

utterances.speaker: NASIHA NESLANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you recall how many?

utterances.speaker: NASIHA NESLANOVIC
utterances.text: He had two bodyguards who escorted him, who accompanied him always, waited for him when he attended meetings, and they were armed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you recognise either of the bodyguards? Were they from Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: NASIHA NESLANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, one of them was from Busovaca, and another one came from Kresevo. The former one wore a multi-coloured uniform and a short rifle, and the latter one had black clothing, white belt, and the holster was also white, the pistol holster. I don't know what you call it, but that was white. The white belt and the black uniform, the one from Kresevo, that is how he was dressed. And I saw him later on at the police station. When he was not with Dario, he was at the police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Looking at the period of June or perhaps early July of 1992, did you observe any special military measures taken by the HVO in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: NASIHA NESLANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean since 1992, in 19 --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In, yes. Did you observe any special military measures taken by the HVO in Busovaca, and if so, against whom were these measures directed?

utterances.speaker: NASIHA NESLANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Sometime in July, on Tihomira Jovica Street, where the majority of residents were Muslim, practically the whole street was Muslim. And in Kadica Mahala, there were also Muslim residents, and their machine-gun nests were set up there and soldiers who manned them and controlled that street. Several times in daytime, a small dump truck would come in with a far-ranging weapon and it would patrol the streets several times a day, both these streets, from one machine-gun nest to another. They would pass, they would drive by and intimidate us; that is how we understood it, to instill fear in us, because there was no other ethnic group but Muslims there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If you recall, do you know at whom the machine-guns in the nests were directed, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: NASIHA NESLANOVIC
utterances.text: They were directed at Muslim houses, because all those houses were Muslim. So they were aiming at those houses, not in front, not behind; either to the left or to the right, depending on whether they were coming back or going.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you recall, were they always manned or -- I'm sorry. Were they manned at all times?

utterances.speaker: NASIHA NESLANOVIC
utterances.text: At that particular period of time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think if this were to be the end of today's session, this would be a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I think we've heard about -- we've heard evidence, quite a lot of it, about the takeover of Busovaca, so it may be convenient to start at paragraph 7 tomorrow, with the 25th of January, '93.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, there are some points in 6. I agree that a good deal has been given. There are some points that I believe have never been brought up in Court, and if I may just selectively ask questions from there, getting past the bulk of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Neslanovic, we are adjourning today. I hope you've been told that it may not be possible to hear your evidence tomorrow first thing because there's another urgent witness to be heard, and I hope you'll bear with us while that's done. But we shall deal with your evidence as soon as we possibly can so that you can finish within a few days. Could you remember, in this adjournment and any others there may be in this case, don't speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include members of the Prosecution. So could you be back, please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you be back, please, when you're told.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until tomorrow at half past 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 4.15 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 7th day of December, 1999, at 9.30 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25
